source.title: kadiak.org — Kodiak Alaska Military History (Chiniak Tour, March 21, 1998)
source.label: kadiak.org — Chiniak Tour (1998)
source.note: Tour photos by Curt Law, AL7LQ (21 March 1998); text by Joe Stevens; comments from veterans as posted on the page.

t01.caption: 1 - The USCG installed a differential GPS transmitter circa 1997 just beside the Miller Field runway. In 1998 the runway condition was severely potholed and some of the rusty Marston matting has been partially removed. It is NOT suitable for landing an airplane. Don Parker: -- The Chiniak DGPS is on 313.0 Khz, with data at 100 baud. Pete Azzole: -- When I was there, Miller Field was merely steel matting. I don't recall finding any structures or remnants thereof in the immediate vacinity of the field. The Army quonset community in the trees shown on my homepage was nearby though. In fact, I never knew it was called "Miller Field" -- I assume we are talking about the same place; it was near our site, maybe 1-2 miles toward the Naval Station.
t01.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)

t02.caption: 2 - Looking north from the DGPS transmitter, you can just make out the WW2 gun emplacement bunker on top of the hill in the distance across the lagoon. Pete Azzole: -- This appears to be the gun emplacement I show in my homepage; the one with the underground command center. [Note: it was just for ammunition storage.]
t02.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)

t04.caption: 4 - The electrical panels in the building suggest quite a lot of power consumption. There are three engine generator exhaust ports from the building. The west end of the building has been demolished, apparently by materials scavengers. These power panels were certainly upgraded several times over the lifetime of this building.
t04.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)

t05.caption: 5 - The inside of the concrete room showing the parallel holes. Best guess is they were for parallel feedlines to antennas.
t05.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)

t06.caption: 6 - View of the east end of the building showing the outside of the concrete room. The wood portion of the building is covered with green painted cedar shakes just like the building below.
t06.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)

t07.caption: 7 - About a half mile south of the above building. The remaining wood is charred suggesting that this building burned down. Pete Azzole: -- This is the remains of the "D/F shack" where the direction finding equipment was located. Chuck Mackey: -- Fred Zharoff taught school in this building. It was windowless and I installed a window for them. Thomas L. Lyon : -- The first year it was used for [a school was] 1967-68.
t07.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)

t08.caption: 8 - There is a remnant of what might be an entrance porch on the right side.
t08.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)

t09.caption: 9 - Just to the west of the building there is this concrete hole in the ground. There is some resemblance to a well, but there are remains of copper parts inside. Lloyd Johnson: -- This is the foundation for the HF DF (HuffDuff) that I operated in 1945.
t09.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)

t11.caption: 11 - Just about a quarter of a mile north of the main Navy building, at the crossroads, there is a very small log cabin. The south end has been extended with frame construction. Pete Azzole: -- Based on your location description, I'm not sure this existed when I was there. I remember a very small cabin which was an escape used by the XO and CO of the Naval Station, but I think it was further away from our site and I'm not sure it was log cabin construction, rather frame/clapboard. Richard Kivi : --That's not the CWO's hideaway. It is an abandoned cabin. We used it one summer to board horses and one of the guys kept his pet raven there. We also used it to dress out some deer we shot that had wondered onto the antenna fields. . . which were also used by a local rancher to graze cattle. [18 July 2007]
t11.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)

t14.caption: 14 - The window glass is missing and the door is gone, all the copper wire has been stripped except for the motor windings. A stream of water is flowing out of the doorway by itself on this day, but it has rained for the last 45 days steadily.
t14.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)

t15.caption: 15 - This and subsequent pictures are of the big log house near the lagoon. This is a short drive from the main road and it is not visible from the main road. Pete Azzole: -- This is the log cabin we all built during my tour as an escape from the barracks environment. (See my homepage) The sounds from the "bar" and combined purpose rec room/mess deck (shown in my homepage) in the barracks carried all too well topside where we slept and especially down the hall where the OIC and Asst. OIC rooms were located. We ran basic power and water to the cabin; had hardly any furniture; we took sleeping bags over there to crash onto. We had a refrigerator, a record player, a soda fountain/ice cream freezer, austere "kitchen" and burned wood to keep warm. The cabin was located a short walk uphill from the lake, which would freeze over and make some great skating. Ted Nelson : -- My daughter was married in this cabin in May 1973.
t15.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)

t16.caption: 16 - Some of the wall has been vandalized but much of the interior is still in place.
t16.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)

t17.caption: 17 - The roof is partially missing and the logs are severly waterlogged. See comments below from Richard Loden.
t17.credit: Photo: Curt Law, AL7LQ, 21 March 1998 (via kadiak.org)
